scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Hustle began in late 1972 when Puerto Rican teenagers in the South Bronx created a 5-step dance with no turns, directly reacting against elders who objected to a grinding slow dance called the 500.
It was initially shared at hooky gigs, house parties, and basement clubs.

In 1973, musician Joe Bataan witnessed this early 6-step movement at the Bronx club '310 1/2' and recorded 'Latin Strut', whose faster tempo inspired teenagers to add fancier gyrations, transforming it into the Latin hustle.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The Hustle served as a youthful social rebellion against parental restrictions on slow grinding dances, quickly transforming into a tool for community peacemaking.
Members of the Imperial Bachelors street gang ran hustle parties at St. Mary's Recreation Center specifically to curb neighborhood violence in the South Bronx during 1974.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Hustle is danced as a couple dance moving freely over the dance floor rather than following a strict line of dance.
The dance uses a lead-and-follow structure where the leader initiates back-forward steps starting on the left foot without a traditional swing rocking action due to the rapid tempo.

Counting patterns syncopate against 4/4 disco music; common timings include '&1 2 3 &1 2 3' (leader stepping Left-Right, Left, Right), as well as '1, 2 & 3' (Slow-Quick-Quick-Slow), '1&23', '12&3', or '123&'.
Watch for The Basic, Turn, Left Turn.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Hustle is performed to disco and funk music structured in 4/4 meter with an accented, steady pulse on every beat, lacking swing bounce or oscillation.

Landmark songs associated with its development include Joe Bataan's 'Latin Strut' (1973), the Fatback Band's 'Spanish Hustle' (1975–1976), and Van McCoy and the Soul City Symphony's chart-topping instrumental 'The Hustle' (1975).
Listen for the funk bass, drums, horns, strings.
The pulse is 4/4.
Evenly accented four-on-the-floor disco beat without swing oscillation, anchored by driving bass guitar, rhythmic brass, swelling orchestral strings, and up-tempo Latin percussion.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Hustle was historically danced in social and urban settings including South Bronx basements, hooky gigs, house parties, church recreation centers such as St. Mary's Recreation Center, and discotheques like New York City's Adam's Apple and club '310 1/2'.
Instructional vinyl releases like 'New York Hustle Incorporated' featured period disco attire and instructional photos to guide home learners.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key pioneers include Willie 'Marine Boy' Estrada, author of 'The Dancing Gangsters of the South Bronx: Rise of the Latin Hustle'; members of the Imperial Bachelors gang; Billy Fajardo and the performance team Disco Dance Dimensions; Latin Symbolics; television producer Marty Angelo, who created 'Disco Step-by-Step' and the Hustle Hall of Fame (later managed by Ron Bess and Mark James); musician Joe Bataan; DJ David Todd; songwriter Van McCoy; producer Charlie Kipps Jr.; and choreographer Deney Terrio.
The dance emerged as the Latin Hustle or Spanish Hustle in the South Bronx, characterized by a 5-step count that evolved into a 6-step pattern.
Hustle shares technical and stylistic ancestry with Mambo, Salsa, and single-step Swing, while integrating the undulating torso and hip isolations of son cubano.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Hustle is parent of Mambo: Hustle shares steps and rotational movement concepts directly with Mambo.
Hustle is parent of Salsa: Cuban immigrants integrated salsa footwork and Latin hip motion into disco dancing to shape the Latin hustle.
Hustle is influence of Swing: Hustle incorporates basic foot mechanics and figures like the inside loop turn and wrap from swing, but places the rock step at the start.
Hustle is sibling of Discofox: Emerging in Europe around the same era, Discofox shares similar basic step structures with Hustle.

scenes.title: Body and posture
narration: Upright, mobile social partner stance allowing rapid rotational momentum and free spatial travel across the floor.
Single or double hand-holds; bellows-like arm pumping during the Wheel figure; high arm arch allowing 360-degree counterclockwise spins in the Inside/Loop Turn; wrap and two-hand switch positions.
Smooth, undulating Cuban-derived hip movement during counts 2 and 3 that should feel soft without exaggerated impact.

scenes.title: Step A — slowly
narration: Step 1: Leader steps back on the left foot, followed by a forward replacement step on the right foot (&1 count)
Step 2: Leader steps forward or sideways on the left foot (count 2)

Footwork from the sources: Leader begins back-forward steps with the left foot (&1 or 1, 2), stepping without swinging or rocking due to high speed; follower executes natural opposite footwork; count patterns include '&1 2 3', '1, 2 & 3', '1&23', '12&3', or '123&'.

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer

scenes.title: Common mistakes and what to avoid
narration: Avoid rocking back on the heels during the rock-step; avoid jerky or over-accentuated hip hits on counts 2 and 3; avoid dancing with swing-style delayed bounce.
Teachers of this dance warn against: putting all weight on the rock step
on_screen: Side-by-side: source-supported correction

Options card: Seated or supported option: Perform the '&1 2 3' foot rhythm seated by tapping the left heel and toe on '&1', followed by alternate flat foot steps on 2 and 3, mimicking the arm bellows of the Wheel with hands clasped. · For children: 'The Bellows Wheel Challenge': Partners link hands and try to steer together like a ship's wheel for 180 degrees before freezing on the count of 3.
